papers.title: Superheavy gravitational dark matter from runaway bubble collisions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30113v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proposes that a particle coupling only gravitationally is pair-produced when runaway bubble walls collide during a first-order phase transition, yielding a flat relic abundance up to masses near 10^17 GeV at low reheating temperatures.
summary.plain: The paper asks how very heavy dark matter could be made in the early universe, when a vacuum bubble expands and its walls collide. The idea is that a hidden particle interacting only through gravity can be created in pairs when these fast-moving walls hit, with no other forces needed. The text reports an estimated yield for a Dirac fermion (a common type of particle) that stays roughly constant up to very large masses, enough to account for dark matter up to about 10^17 GeV even when the universe was reheated to temperatures far below that mass.
summary.why: It offers a route to dark matter far heavier than the usual freeze-in mechanism can reach, using gravity as the only link to the Standard Model. The text does not say how the result compares with observations or whether the bubble scenario is realised, so its relevance to real dark matter remains an open question.
summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the matter in the universe, inferred from its gravitational pull.
- Vacuum bubbles: in some models of the early universe, regions of space tunnel into a lower-energy state and expand as bubbles; their walls can run away, accelerating toward light speed.
- Graviton exchange: gravity is carried by a hypothetical particle, the graviton; here it is the only force linking the bubble walls to the dark particle.
- Yield: the number of dark particles produced per unit of entropy (a measure of the hot material's disorder), which sets how much dark matter remains.
- Reheating temperature: the temperature the universe reached after inflation ended and its energy was converted into hot particles.
- Freeze-in: a production mechanism where particles are slowly created by ordinary collisions in the hot early universe; the text says it fails for these very heavy masses.
- Planck mass: the natural mass scale of gravity (about 10^19 GeV).

papers.abstract: A stable particle that couples only through gravity is pair-produced in collisions of runaway bubble walls by graviton exchange. For a transition of duration $1/\beta$, a Dirac fermion reaches the yield $Y_X\simeq6.8\times10^{-3}(H/\beta)(T_{\rm reh}/M_{\rm P})^3$, where $H$ is the Hubble rate of the vacuum energy, $T_{\rm reh}$ the reheating temperature and $M_{\rm P}$ the reduced Planck mass. The yield is flat up to masses near $(H/\beta)M_{\rm P}/\nu^2$, where $\nu$ of order one sets the wall-field excursion. Gravity alone then gives dark matter up to about $10^{17}$~GeV at reheating temperatures far below its mass, where freeze-in fails.

papers.title: WIMPs as FIMPs: the Inert Doublet Model and low-temperature reheating
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28217v1

summary.one_liner: The paper revisits the Inert Doublet Model, showing that low reheating temperatures can stop a WIMP dark matter candidate from reaching chemical equilibrium, so its relic abundance comes from freeze-in rather than freeze-out, including instantaneous and finite-duration reheating scenarios.
summary.plain: The paper asks how dark matter particles could have been produced in the early universe, a question usually answered by assuming they were once in thermal balance and then "froze out" as the universe cooled. The authors show that if the universe was reheated to only a low temperature after inflation, a heavy dark matter candidate in the Inert Doublet Model may never reach that balance and instead gets produced gradually, a process called freeze-in. They describe several possible production histories and report that this opens parameter regions that would otherwise be ruled out because they produce too much dark matter.
summary.why: It suggests that the standard assumption linking a WIMP's abundance to its interaction strength may not hold, which matters for how dark matter searches are interpreted. The text does not show experimental consequences, so the broader significance remains to be tested.
summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter whose gravity explains galaxy motions; its total amount is measured.
- WIMP (weakly interacting massive particle): a heavy dark matter candidate that is produced through its interactions with ordinary particles.
- Thermal freeze-out: the particle is in balance with the hot plasma, then drops out as the universe expands and cools, leaving a fixed leftover amount.
- Freeze-in: the particle is produced very weakly and gradually, never reaching balance; this is typical of FIMPs (feebly interacting particles).
- Reheating: the hot phase of the universe after inflation; its temperature sets the early thermal history.
- Inert Doublet Model: an extension of the Standard Model Higgs sector that contains a dark matter candidate.
- Relic abundance: the amount of dark matter left over today.

papers.abstract: Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) are conventionally assumed to acquire their dark matter relic abundance through thermal freeze-out. However, this association relies on assumptions concerning the thermal history of the early Universe. We revisit the Inert Doublet Model (IDM), a representative WIMP framework in which dark matter interacts with the Standard Model through electroweak gauge interactions, even when its Higgs-portal coupling vanishes. We demonstrate that sufficiently low reheating temperatures can prevent chemical equilibrium, allowing a genuine WIMP to acquire its relic abundance through freeze-in rather than freeze-out. Considering both instantaneous and finite-duration reheating, we identify different production histories, including freeze-out during radiation domination, freeze-out during reheating, and freeze-in with potentially significant annihilation backreactions. These scenarios open regions of the IDM parameter space that would otherwise be excluded by dark matter overabundance. Our results demonstrate that WIMPs can behave as FIMPs, depending on the thermal history of the Universe.

papers.title: Dark matter mass fraction in axion stars
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30321v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies, detected only through gravity.
- QCD axion: a hypothetical very light particle proposed to solve a puzzle in the strong nuclear force; a candidate for dark matter.
- Minicluster: a small, dense clump of axion dark matter formed early in the universe.
- Bose-Einstein condensation: a state where many identical light particles all occupy the same quantum state, acting like one big wave.
- Bose star: a gravitationally bound, self-gravitating blob of such a condensate.
- Mass fraction and mass function: the share of total dark matter in these stars, and how many stars exist at each mass.
summary.one_liner: Using an recently derived analytic solution for how Bose stars grow inside QCD axion miniclusters, this paper estimates the present-day fraction of dark matter bound in Bose stars and their resulting mass function.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a proposed form of dark matter made of very light particles called axions. In this picture, the dark matter clumps into small, dense blobs, and inside those blobs it may condense into compact "Bose stars," which are like giant quantum clouds. The authors use a previously published mathematical solution for how these stars grow to work out how much of today's dark matter ends up locked in them and how their sizes are distributed.
summary.why: If dark matter is largely in these compact stars, that would change predictions for how it clusters and for any signals from detectors or astrophysical observations. The text does not state the actual fraction or mass values, so the size of the effect is not clear from the abstract alone, and its link to observations is not described here.

papers.abstract: QCD axion dark matter is fragmented into small mass miniclusters of high density. With the natural parameters of miniclusters, the time for Bose-Einstein condensation is less than the age of the Universe, which leads to the formation of Bose stars inside these structures. Recently, the problem of the subsequent growth of Bose stars was solved analytically (Dmitriev et al, Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 091001 (2024)). We use this solution to determine present day mass fraction of dark matter in Bose stars and their mass function.

papers.title: Scotogenic dark matter from gauged $L_\mu+L_\tau$
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28223v1

summary.background:
- Standard Model: the established theory of known particles and forces.
- Neutrino mass: neutrinos have very small masses; Majorana nature means a neutrino is its own antiparticle.
- Scotogenic model: a scheme where neutrino masses arise from a loop of new particles, with a dark matter candidate in that loop.
- Gauged symmetry: a conserved quantity promoted to a force carrier, here L_mu + L_tau (muon and tau lepton numbers), whose boson is the Z'.
- Matter parity: a leftover symmetry (like a sign ±1 for particles) that makes the lightest odd particle stable.
- WIMP: weakly interacting massive particle, a common dark matter candidate with a thermal relic abundance.
- Kinetic mixing: a small coupling between the new force's field and the ordinary photon field, parameterized by epsilon.
- Electroweak precision constraints: high-precision measurements of W, Z and related quantities that limit new physics.
- Leptophilic: a particle that couples mainly to leptons.
summary.one_liner: A proposed "scotogenic" extension of the Standard Model, built on a gauged L_mu + L_tau lepton-number symmetry, that generates small Majorana neutrino masses at one loop and provides a weakly interacting dark matter candidate stabilized by a remnant matter parity, with analysis of its scalar dark matter, Z' boson, and collider constraints.
summary.plain: The paper proposes a theoretical model in which the tiny masses of neutrinos and the invisible dark matter in the universe share a common origin. A new force carrier (Z') linked to the difference between muon-type and tau-type lepton numbers is introduced, and its symmetry breaking leaves behind a leftover "parity" that keeps the lightest new particle from decaying. The authors study which parameter choices give a dark matter abundance matching observations, and check the model against precision electroweak measurements, existing searches for leptophilic gauge bosons, and possible collider signals.
summary.why: It offers a single framework that links two open problems, neutrino mass and dark matter, through a new gauge boson that could be tested in experiments. The text does not show how strongly the model is favored over alternatives, so its relevance to real data remains to be judged by further work.

papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce the first scotogenic model based on a gauged $L_{\mu} + L_{\tau}$ symmetry whose spontaneous breaking by two units leaves a remnant matter parity $M_P$. The resulting light active neutrinos are of Majorana nature and the lightest electrically neutral state mediating the scotogenic loop is stabilized by $M_P$ and can be identified as a weakly interacting massive particle dark matter candidate. We analyze the phenomenology of a predominantly singlet-like CP-even scalar dark matter candidate and the representative regions of parameter space compatible with the observed thermal relic abundance. The $Z'$ boson is compatible with a broad range of parameters relevant for dark matter. In particular, electroweak precision constraints do not lead to significant tensions for kinetic mixing values up to $\epsilon\sim 10^{-2}$. We discuss the implications of existing searches for leptophilic gauge bosons and the conditions under which visible and invisible collider signatures become relevant.

papers.title: Probing Compressed Dark Sectors at a Muon Collider through Dilepton Signatures and Machine Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27518v1

summary.background:
- Standard Model: the current theory of known particles and forces.
- Inert doublet model: a simple extension adding a second Higgs-like field; its lightest neutral new particle can be dark matter.
- Dark matter relic abundance: the amount of dark matter left over from the early universe; the model struggles to match the observed amount in some mass ranges.
- Compressed spectrum: new particles with very similar masses, so their decay products are soft and hard to detect.
- Muon collider: a proposed future machine colliding muons and antimuons, offering cleaner collisions than proton machines.
- Dilepton signature: a pair of leptons (electron or muon pairs) used as the detectable trace of the event.
- BDT / XGBoost: machine-learning methods that combine many decision rules to separate signal from background.
- Off-shell Z* : a virtual Z boson, not on its mass shell, produced in the decay chain.
summary.one_liner: A study proposing that machine-learning classifiers (BDT and XGBoost) applied to dilepton final states at a future muon collider could help find inert-doublet scalar dark matter in compressed mass spectra via the process μ+μ− → AH, A → HZ*, Z* → ℓ+ℓ−.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a possible dark matter particle, a hidden heavier cousin of the Higgs in a simple extension of the Standard Model, could be spotted at a future muon collider. The idea is that two heavy partner particles are made in muon collisions, one decays into the other plus a virtual Z boson, and that Z decays to a pair of leptons. Machine-learning tools are used to pick this signal out from ordinary background events.
summary.why: Dark matter that is only slightly heavier-or-lighter than its partner ("compressed" spectra) is hard to see at existing colliders, so a cleaner collider with machine-learning analysis is one proposed route to search for it. The text does not report sensitivity numbers or specific results, so how strong the claimed discovery potential is cannot be judged from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: The inert doublet model (IDM), a minimal extension of the Standard Model (SM), provides a scalar dark matter (DM) candidate that belongs to the additional Higgs doublet. The model faces challenges in achieving the correct relic abundance for compressed spectra and DM masses in the high-mass range. In this work we investigate the prospects of detecting dark matter candidates at future high-energy muon colliders. Focusing on the process $\mu^+ \mu^- \to AH$ with subsequent decay $A \to H Z^*$ and $Z^* \to \ell^+\ell^-$, we explore the sensitivity of machine learning techniques, specifically Boosted Decision Trees (BDT) and XGBoost, to distinguish the signal from Standard Model backgrounds. We demonstrate that the combination of advanced multivariate analysis with high-luminosity muon collisions enhances the discovery potential for inert scalars in compressed mass spectra scenarios.

papers.title: From Resonance Properties to High-Energy Behavior: The $R$ Ratio from Lattice QCD
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27586v1

summary.background:
- QCD (quantum chromodynamics) is the theory of the strong force binding quarks and gluons.
- Lattice QCD simulates that theory on a discrete grid of space and time on computers.
- The R-ratio is the ratio of hadron production to muon-pair production in electron-positron collisions; it probes the strong force across energies.
- A resonance (here the rho meson) is a short-lived particle seen as a peak in the energy spectrum; f_rho is its decay constant, a measure of how strongly it couples to its decay channel.
- Euclidean correlators are simulation outputs in imaginary time that must be mathematically converted (via Bayesian reconstruction) back to real-energy spectra.
- Finite-volume effects are distortions caused by simulating in a box of finite size.
- A Gaussian smearing with width sigma is a broadening applied to compare lattice and experimental spectra on equal footing.
summary.one_liner: A lattice QCD study that uses Bayesian spectral reconstruction of Euclidean correlators near the physical pion mass to extract the R-ratio, the rho-peak decay constant f_rho, and a Gaussian-smeared R-ratio compared against experiment, with finite-volume effects examined across ensembles.
summary.plain: This paper uses supercomputer simulations of the strong force that binds quarks into protons and pions to predict how often electrons and positrons colliding at high energy turn into hadrons, a quantity called the R-ratio. The authors reconstruct the particle-production spectrum from simulated data and compare it with experimental measurements. They report that the reconstruction matches the smooth high-energy trend seen in experiment, and that the rho resonance's decay constant comes out close to the experimental value.
summary.why: Computing this kind of inclusive quantity directly from the underlying theory is hard, so a method that reproduces both the resonance peak and the broad high-energy behavior is of interest to lattice QCD and hadron physics. The text does not establish how this compares with other lattice approaches, and its claimed applications to other channels and decay rates are stated as potential only.

papers.abstract: We investigate resonance properties and inclusive spectral behavior through Bayesian reconstruction of the $R$-ratio from Euclidean lattice correlators near the physical pion mass. Without additional Gaussian smearing, the reconstructed spectrum already captures the smooth high-energy behavior observed in experiment. Direct integration of the $\rho$ peak determines $f_\rho$ with approximately $1\%$ statistical precision and close agreement with the experimental reference, providing access to resonance properties without resolving individual finite-volume levels. With a common Gaussian width of $\sigma=0.6$~GeV, the lattice and experimental $R$-ratios show good overall agreement over $0.25$--$2.50$~GeV. Comparisons among ensembles with spatial extents up to approximately $10$~fm demonstrate that finite-volume effects can be controlled across these complementary observables. These results demonstrate a unified framework for studying resonance and inclusive physics from lattice QCD, with potential applications to other hadronic channels, inclusive decay rates, and hadronic tensors.

papers.title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25359v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that is inferred from its gravity; its particle identity is unknown.
- Sub-halo: a smaller, dense clump of dark matter within a larger dark matter halo.
- Pulsar timing: precise tracking of the regular pulses from spinning neutron stars; tiny unexpected drifts can reveal nearby gravity.
- Acceleration measured outside the tidal radius: the data only sense the total pull from outside the object, so the interior structure cannot be read off.
- Candidate models named in the text: ultralight wave dark matter, warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter, primordial black holes, and others.
- LUX-ZEPLIN: an underground detector searching for dark matter particles by their recoils.
- Cusp vs. core: whether density rises sharply toward the centre or stays flat.
summary.one_liner: A theory-organized survey of what a candidate dark matter sub-halo near the Sun, inferred from pulsar-timing accelerations, would imply for dark matter models, and which future measurements could tell those models apart.
summary.plain: Timing signals from distant pulsars (rapidly spinning dead stars) seem to be nudged by a hidden concentration of mass near the Sun, which could be a clump of dark matter. The paper goes through many candidate dark matter types and asks what each would predict for that clump. It then lists four kinds of new observations that could tell the candidates apart, since the current data cannot.
summary.why: If a dark matter clump is really this close to Earth, it would be a rare direct handle on what dark matter is made of, which is an open question in physics. The text is a framework and does not establish that the clump exists, so its value depends on whether the pulsar-timing signal holds up.

papers.abstract: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.

papers.title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo for dark matter production and phase-space evolution
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25812v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies; its origin is studied through its early-universe history.
- Freeze-out: the point when particles stop interacting enough to keep up with the cooling universe, fixing how many remain.
- Boltzmann equations: equations that track how many particles exist and how their energies are spread out over time.
- Phase space: the combined description of where particles are and how fast they move; here, the distribution of momenta.
- Thermal equilibrium: a state where particles share a common temperature-set energy spread; out-of-equilibrium means this does not hold.
- Monte Carlo method: estimating results by simulating many random events and averaging them.
- Bimodal distribution: a distribution with two distinct peaks.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces Direct Simulation Monte Carlo, a particle-based stochastic method, to solve phase-space Boltzmann equations for dark matter production, freeze-out, decays, and scattering without a fixed momentum grid or thermally averaged cross sections.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how dark matter particles could have been produced in the hot early universe and how their speeds and energies evolved afterwards. Instead of tracking the full distribution of particle energies on a fixed grid, the authors simulate a large group of individual particles that collide and change at random according to probabilities. They test the method on a scenario with two production steps, which gives a two-peaked energy distribution, and show how it handles scattering and particle-number changes.
summary.why: Dark matter abundance and its speed distribution affect how structure forms in the universe, so more flexible tools for these calculations matter. The text presents the method as a general approach for out-of-equilibrium cases, but it does not report a broader comparison with existing solvers, so its practical advantage is not established here.

papers.abstract: To study the early-universe production of dark matter particles beyond thermal equilibrium often requires solving several coupled Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level. We present a new method to address this challenge using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) based on stochastic interactions of an ensemble of particles. We implement and validate efficient algorithms to describe freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes within the dark sector. These algorithms do not require a discretisation of momentum space on a pre-defined grid and do not rely on approximations such as thermally averaged cross sections. As illustrative example, we consider a scenario with two-step dark matter production, leading to a bimodal phase-space distribution, and consider the subsequent evolution under elastic and number-changing processes. We show that DSMC is a flexible approach to explore out-of-equilibrium processes and solve Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level in order to predict the abundance of dark matter particles and their effect on structure formation.

papers.title: Positron escape from dark matter spikes in black hole X-ray binaries
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23983v1

summary.background:
- AMS-02: a particle detector on the International Space Station that measures cosmic rays, including positrons.
- Positron excess: more positrons observed at high energies than standard models of cosmic-ray production predict.
- Dark matter annihilation: hypothetical dark matter particles colliding and destroying each other, producing ordinary particles such as positrons.
- Dark matter spike: a dense, steeply peaked concentration of dark matter that can form around a black hole.
- X-ray binary: a system where a black hole or neutron star pulls matter from a companion star, emitting X-rays; A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480 are two nearby examples.
- Diffusion-loss equation: the standard equation describing how charged particles spread out through magnetic fields while losing energy.
- Event horizon: the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape.
- Cross-section: a measure of how likely particles are to interact; a larger required cross-section means the proposed process must be far more frequent.
summary.one_liner: A comment arguing that a dark-matter-annihilation explanation for the AMS-02 positron excess, based on spike halos around nearby black hole X-ray binaries, fails once the magnetic and diffusive environment near the black hole horizon is modelled accurately.
summary.plain: Cosmic-ray detectors such as AMS-02 on the International Space Station have measured more positrons (anti-electrons) arriving from space than simple models predict. One proposed explanation is that dark matter particles annihilate in dense clumps around nearby black holes and produce these positrons. This paper challenges that idea: the authors argue that the magnetic environment very close to a black hole changes how positrons escape, and that once this is included, the required dark matter annihilation rate would need to be hundreds to over a thousand times larger.
summary.why: The positron excess is one of the long-running hints that dark matter might be detectable through cosmic rays, so whether a specific proposed source survives scrutiny matters for that search. The text does not show how robust the factor of roughly 500 to 1400 is across all plausible models, so the conclusion should be read as the authors' estimate rather than settled fact.

papers.abstract: Chan and Lee present a model where the AMS-02 positron excess is explained by dark matter (DM) annihilation in spike halos around nearby black holes A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480. Their model assumes a uniform magnetic and diffusive environment en route to Earth. Thus, it depends on the assumption that one can ignore the small-scale, near-horizon environment in the diffusion-loss equation. We demonstrate that this is not the case. An accurate magnetic field model near the horizon means, without increasing the required cross-section by a factor of roughly 500 to 1400, depending on the transport near the horizon, the positron flux from these sources cannot account for a significant fraction of the AMS-02 excess.

papers.title: Measurements of the total and differential inclusive electron neutrino charged-current cross sections on argon with SBND
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25098v1

summary.one_liner: A measurement, using the SBND detector at Fermilab's Booster Neutrino Beam, of the total and single-differential inclusive electron-neutrino (plus antineutrino) charged-current cross sections on argon, compared against common neutrino event generators.
summary.plain: This paper reports how often neutrinos of a specific type (electron neutrinos) interact with argon atoms when they hit a detector, and how that rate depends on the energy and angle of the electron that comes out. The team used the SBND detector at Fermilab, collecting data equal to about 8.81 × 10^19 protons aimed at a target, and selected 729 candidate events. They found a total interaction rate of about 3.90 × 10^-39 cm² per nucleon, and they report that the data favor simulation tools that predict a lower overall rate.
summary.why:
Neutrino experiments that look for oscillations, where neutrinos change type, depend on accurate models of how neutrinos interact, so direct measurements of this channel help check those models. The text links the result to future long- and short-baseline oscillation searches and to searches for physics beyond the Standard Model, but it does not itself show what effect the result will have on those searches.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Neutrinos: nearly massless, electrically neutral particles that interact very rarely with matter.
- Charged-current interaction: a neutrino exchanges a charged W boson with a nucleus and turns into a charged lepton (here an electron).
- Cross section: a measure of how likely an interaction is, expressed as an effective target area; the unit cm² per nucleon is per nucleon in the target.
- Argon: the liquid detector material used in SBND.
- Booster Neutrino Beam: a beam of neutrinos produced at Fermilab.
- Neutrino event generators: computer programs that simulate neutrino interactions; the paper compares its data with them.
- Oscillation: neutrinos changing from one type to another as they travel, which requires knowing interaction rates accurately.
- Statistical vs. systematic uncertainty: random counting error vs. errors from detector and modeling assumptions.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

papers.abstract: This work presents measurements of the total and single-differential electron neutrino charged-current cross sections on argon using the Short-Baseline Near Detector (SBND) at Fermilab. We present the highest statistics inclusive $ν_e + \bar ν_e$ (95.2% $ν_e$ and 4.8% $\barν_e$) charged-current cross section measurement on argon to date and the first inclusive $ν_e + \bar ν_e$ cross section measurement using the Booster Neutrino Beam. Direct measurements of this channel are crucial for future studies of both long- and short-baseline neutrino oscillations through electron neutrino appearance, which in turn are vital for answering open questions in neutrino phenomenology and searching for beyond the Standard Model physics at the intensity frontier. The data used for this work were collected with an exposure of $8.81 \times10^{19}$ protons on target, and 729 candidate events are selected with a minimum electron energy of 500 MeV. The single-differential cross sections are extracted in electron energy and angle with respect to the beam axis. The flux-averaged total cross section is measured to be $σ= [3.90 \pm 0.18\,\text{(stat)} \pm 0.41\,\text{(syst)}] \times 10^{-39}$ cm$^2$/nucleon for a predicted average neutrino energy of $\langle E_ν\rangle=1.8$ GeV for selected events. The total and differential cross sections are compared to predictions from common neutrino event generators. The data show a preference for generators that predict a lower overall cross section.

papers.title: A Universal Axion in a Twin-QCD Sector
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23015v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies, inferred from gravity.
- QCD (quantum chromodynamics): the theory of the strong force that binds quarks into protons and neutrons.
- Strong-CP problem: QCD allows a symmetry-breaking term that experiments have not seen; an axion is a hypothetical particle that would explain why it is effectively zero.
- Axion mass: the axion's mass is set by QCD; a larger mass changes how much axion dark matter is produced.
- Twin sector: a hypothetical hidden copy of the Standard Model's strong force with its own particles and confinement scale.
- Baryons: heavy particles like protons and neutrons, made of three quarks.
- Lattice QCD: a computer method for solving strong-force physics numerically; "lattice-informed" means its results are used as inputs.
- Two-temperature description: modelling the visible and hidden sectors as having different temperatures in the early universe.
- Baryon asymmetry: the small excess of matter over antimatter produced early on.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical study proposing a single axion coupled to both ordinary QCD and a mirror "twin" QCD sector, where the enhanced axion mass and twin baryons form a mixed dark-matter scenario, with lattice-informed estimates and a two-temperature early-universe treatment.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether dark matter could be made of two things at once: a light particle called the axion and a heavier kind of matter built from a hidden "twin" version of the strong force that holds atomic nuclei together. The authors show that adding this hidden sector can raise the axion's mass, for example by about a factor of 25 in one illustrative case, while still solving the strong-CP problem, a puzzle about why a certain symmetry is not violated in nuclear physics. They then estimate how much of the dark matter each component could supply under chosen assumptions.
summary.why: It offers a quantitative framework for mixed dark-matter models and spells out conditions the scenario must meet, including limits from the early-universe thermal history and from structure formation. The results are conditional on chosen benchmark values, so they should be read as a proposal to be tested rather than an established finding.

papers.abstract: Dark matter may consist of multiple components with distinct particle-physics origins. We investigate a scenario in which a universal axion couples to both visible and twin QCD, with twin baryons providing a possible dominant dark-matter component. The presence of a second strongly interacting sector can substantially enhance the axion mass while preserving its role in resolving the strong-CP problem, provided the physical vacuum angles are appropriately aligned. For a representative uniformly rescaled twin spectrum with a confinement scale five times that of ordinary QCD, the axion mass is enhanced by approximately a factor of 25. Using lattice-informed QCD results and a two-temperature description of the early universe, we investigate the cosmological evolution and relative abundances of the dark-sector components. In a representative conditional numerical benchmark, axions account for a small percentage of the observed dark matter, while twin baryons could constitute the remainder for a suitable primordial baryon asymmetry. We also examine the implications for additional relativistic species, strong-CP alignment, and the interactions of stable twin matter. Our results provide a quantitative framework for exploring mixed axion--twin-baryon dark matter and identify the particle-physics and cosmological conditions necessary for a viable realization, including constraints from the thermal history and formation of cosmic structure.

papers.title: Leading Axion Sensitivity with Interstellar Medium Optical Line Emission
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23385v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects; its composition is unknown.
- Axion: a hypothetical light particle proposed to solve a problem in particle physics and as a dark matter candidate.
- Axion coupling: how strongly an axion interacts with photons (light) or electrons; the paper constrains these couplings.
- Decay: an unstable particle transforming into other particles; here axions decaying to photons or electrons.
- Ionization threshold: the minimum energy needed to strip an electron from an atom; the paper covers axion masses below this for hydrogen.
- H-alpha: a specific red optical emission line of hydrogen, at a fixed wavelength.
- Leo T: a small, faint dwarf galaxy, rich in dark matter relative to its light.
- Constraint/limit: an upper bound on a parameter, from showing that a signal was not seen.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes using optical hydrogen-alpha emission from the interstellar medium, produced when axion dark matter decays to photons or electrons, as a new probe of axions in the eV-to-GeV mass range, and applies it to Very Large Telescope data from the Leo T galaxy.
summary.plain: Axions are hypothetical very light particles that some physicists think could make up dark matter, the unseen material that holds galaxies together. This paper suggests looking for them through faint light from hydrogen gas in a nearby dwarf galaxy, Leo T: if axions decay, they can knock hydrogen atoms into emitting a specific red glow. Using telescope data from that galaxy, the authors report limits on axion properties that the text describes as strong and covering regions not previously explored.
summary.why: Searches for axion dark matter usually look for signals at energies set by the axion mass, so a channel that emits at a fixed atomic wavelength is a different approach and could cover parameter ranges that are poorly constrained now. The abstract also links the limits to explanations of JWST observations of early supermassive black holes, though the strength of that connection is not something the abstract itself establishes.

papers.abstract: We introduce interstellar optical line emission as a new probe of axion dark matter. Axion decays to photons or electrons can excite or ionize neutral hydrogen, producing H$α$ emission at a fixed atomic wavelength rather than at an energy set by the axion mass. Developing the formalism and applying it to the Leo T galaxy with Very Large Telescope data, we derive strong constraints for eV--GeV scale axions, covering new regions of parameter space for both axion-photon and axion-electron couplings. These results establish optical line measurements as a new discovery channel for axion dark matter, probe poorly constrained parameter space below hydrogen's ionization threshold, and constrain axion explanations of JWST's high-redshift supermassive-black-hole observations.

papers.title: Improved Bounds on the Dark Matter-Neutrino Cross Section using LSBGs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.17922v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter inferred from its gravity on stars and gas; its particle nature is unknown.
- Neutrinos: nearly massless, weakly interacting particles produced in huge numbers in supernovae.
- Elastic scattering: a collision where particles bounce off each other without changing identity; the cross section measures how likely such collisions are.
- Cusp vs. core: dark matter density in simulations often peaks sharply at the centre (cusp); observations sometimes show a flatter centre (core).
- Low surface brightness galaxies (LSBGs): large, dim, diffuse galaxies with low star density, where dark matter is dominant and cores are measured.
- Fornax dSph: the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy, a previously used test system.
- DMDSNB: the dark matter diffuse supernova neutrino background, another way to constrain the same interaction.
- Units: cm² is an area; 10⁻²⁵ cm² is a very small effective target size, and GeV/MeV are energy units.
summary.one_liner: The paper sets new upper limits on the elastic scattering cross section between dark matter and neutrinos, using supernova neutrinos heating the cores of low surface brightness galaxies and correcting a double-counting flaw in earlier versions of the method.
summary.plain: Dark matter is an invisible substance that makes up most of the matter in galaxies, and it is not yet known how strongly it interacts with neutrinos, tiny nearly massless particles. The authors look at neutrinos from exploding stars (supernovae) that could push energy into a galaxy's dark matter and smooth out its dense central peak into a flatter core. Using faint, spread-out galaxies whose dark matter cores are measured, they find that the interaction must be weaker than a stated bound.
summary.why: Limits on how often dark matter and neutrinos collide narrow down what dark matter can be, and this work claims to tighten existing bounds. The main claimed gain is that each dark matter particle is counted only once, which the authors say weakens earlier Fornax-based limits by about a factor of 50; the result is a model-dependent bound at one mass and one neutrino energy, so its robustness depends on the assumptions behind it.

papers.abstract: We derive new constraints on the interaction cross section between dark matter and neutrinos ($σ_{νχ}$) that improve upon existing limits. We adopt a mechanism where neutrinos emitted from core-collapse supernovae transfer their energy to the dark matter halo via elastic scattering, transitioning a centrally cusped profile to a flat-cored profile. We apply this mechanism to Low Surface Brightness Galaxies (LSBGs), which are characterized by their relatively large sizes, low stellar densities, and measurements of dark matter cores. We improve upon previous methods so that each dark matter particle is counted at most once, which weakens existing limits, e.g., from the Fornax dSph by a factor of $\sim 50$. Applying our new method to LSBGs, we derive an upper limit of $σ_{νχ}< 8.5 \times 10^{-25}\,\rm cm^2$ for a dark matter mass of $m_χ=1\,\rm GeV$ at a typical supernova neutrino energy of $E_ν=15\,\rm MeV$. This constraint is approximately three orders of magnitude stronger than the Fornax limit derived with the same method and slightly stronger than the bound from the dark matter diffused supernova neutrino background (DMDSNB).

papers.title: Hunting dark matter: the present and future of direct particle detection
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21052v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects on galaxies and the wider universe; its particle identity is unknown.
- Direct detection: looking for rare collisions of dark matter particles with atoms in a sensitive detector deep underground, where cosmic rays are shielded.
- Nuclear recoil: a dark matter particle knocks an atomic nucleus; electron recoil: it knocks an electron.
- Energy threshold: the smallest energy deposit a detector can register; lower thresholds let it search for lighter dark matter.
- Annual modulation: the expected yearly rise and fall in event rate as Earth's motion through the halo changes with the seasons.
- Directional detection: trying to measure the direction of recoils to pick out the wind of dark matter from the galaxy.
- Background: other signals (radioactivity, cosmic rays, neutrinos) that can mimic a dark matter event.
- Noble liquid: liquids such as xenon or argon used as detection media.
summary.one_liner: A review of direct dark matter detection covering the theory of halo-particle scattering (nuclear, electron, collective excitations, absorption, time and direction signatures), detector technologies, results since 2020, and planned low-threshold and noble-liquid experiments.
summary.plain: Dark matter is thought to make up much of the universe's mass, but no one has yet detected it directly in a lab. This review surveys the experiments that try to catch dark matter particles from our galaxy's halo bumping into ordinary matter in detectors. It summarises the theory behind these searches, the detector technologies used, recent results since 2020, and the next generation of experiments.
summary.why: The text notes that, despite much better sensitivity, no conclusive detection has been made, so a clear map of the current status and remaining challenges is useful for planning. It also flags neutrino-induced background as a growing problem for future searches; the text does not say how far these efforts will go.

papers.abstract: The nature of dark matter remains one of the major open questions in particle physics and cosmology. Direct detection experiments aim to identify dark matter particles through their interactions with ordinary matter, but despite substantial improvements in experimental sensitivity, no conclusive detection has been achieved. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the present status and future prospects of direct particle detection, focusing on searches for dark matter particles from the Galactic halo. We introduce the theoretical framework for interpreting experimental results, including nuclear and electron scattering, collective excitations, particle absorption, and time- and direction-dependent signatures. We review the detection technologies employed in these searches, highlighting their operating principles, advantages, and limitations, as well as the calibration techniques and background mitigation strategies required to achieve high sensitivity. Particular emphasis is placed on experimental results reported since 2020, covering nuclear and electron recoil searches, annual modulation measurements, and directional detection. We also discuss experiments under construction and proposed future detectors, ranging from large-scale noble-liquid experiments to low-threshold technologies targeting sub-GeV dark matter. Finally, we examine the challenges that will shape the next generation of experiments, including the need for increasingly low energy thresholds, improved background understanding and discrimination, and the growing importance of neutrino-induced backgrounds. The diversity and complementarity of detector technologies will remain essential for exploring the dark matter parameter space and establishing the nature of any potential signal.
